$comment: CASE STUDIES — problem → method → artifact → result, with the evidence attached.
The site already told these stories, but as prose: a challenge paragraph, a
list of approaches, a list of outcomes. What a reader could not do was ask
'how do you know?' of any single number. Every `results` entry here
therefore carries a `basis` — how the figure was arrived at — and every
`artifacts` entry carries an availability `status`, because 'I built a
thing' means very little without saying whether anyone can see it.
RULES THIS FILE IS HELD TO (tests/content.test.js enforces them):
· Every claim has a basis. A number with no basis is a boast.
· Every artifact declares status: public | on-request | internal | planned.
Only `public` may carry a url, and that url must resolve — either to a
file in this repository or to a host the repository already trusts.
This is the rule that makes fabricating a link fail the build.
· No publication venue, DOI or journal is named anywhere unless the
artifact genuinely has one. Two theses were examined and defended; that
is what they say, and nothing more.
· `lenses` lists which role-specific views a case study belongs to, and
must reference ids defined in content/lenses.json.

caseStudies.title: Sustainable AI Framework
caseStudies.subtitle: Making a finance ministry's AI adoption accountable for its footprint
caseStudies.organization: Digital Society School, Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences
caseStudies.problem: Generative AI is becoming government infrastructure — but every prompt has a footprint. How does a finance ministry adopt AI responsibly without greenwashing, and without grinding innovation to a halt?
method: Mapped the environmental footprint of generative AI end to end — Scope 2 electricity, Scope 3 hardware, and data-centre water.
Built a sustainability assessment framework for concrete AI use cases, framed against CSRD/ESRS disclosure logic so the output lands in a reporting language the ministry already speaks.
Prototyped decision-support tools with real users at both ends of the organisation: managers setting strategy, and employees writing prompts.
Aligned the framework against UN SDG 12 (responsible consumption and production) and SDG 13 (climate action).

artifacts.name: EcoPrompt Coach — web tool
artifacts.note: Energy, water and carbon per LLM query across named models and grids, with every emission factor's source, range and review date shown in an evidence ledger.

artifacts.name: promptcoach — the research prototype it mirrors
artifacts.note: The Digital Society School prototype. The web tool reproduces its calculation model.

artifacts.name: Sustainability assessment framework for AI use cases
artifacts.heldBy: Digital Society School / Ministry of Finance
artifacts.note: Developed inside a research partnership; not mine to publish unilaterally.

results.claim: A working decision-support prototype, not a slide deck
results.basis: The tool is public and runnable — every number it prints is derived in ai-carbon-data.js, which carries a source, publication date, uncertainty range and review date per factor.

results.claim: Framework tested with users at both ends of the organisation
results.basis: Public research sessions and demo days in Amsterdam, with managers and day-to-day users. Qualitative — no completion or satisfaction metric was collected.

caseStudies.caveat: This work is in progress and the outcome measures are qualitative. Any figure describing adoption or emissions avoided would be a guess, so none is given.

caseStudies.title: Coastal Water Pollution Dynamics
caseStudies.subtitle: What drives river-borne pollution, and what Africa's coasts look like by mid-century
caseStudies.problem: Rivers carry whatever we put in them straight to the sea. How do income, urbanisation and agriculture shape the export of multiple pollutants across the world's sub-basins — and what does that mean for Africa's coasts by mid-century?
method: Modelled river export of multiple pollutants with the MARINA-Multi model across 10,226 sub-basins worldwide.
Identified the socioeconomic drivers behind the resulting pollution patterns statistically.
Built qualitative future storylines for African coastal waters, including a deliberately pessimistic 'Dirty Delta' scenario.
Integrated climate-change scenarios into the projections.

artifacts.name: MSc thesis — socioeconomic drivers of river export of multiple pollutants, and qualitative future storylines for African coastal water pollution
artifacts.note: Examined and defended at Wageningen University & Research. Available on request; not deposited in a public repository.

artifacts.name: Scenario storylines for African coastal waters
artifacts.note: Including the 'Dirty Delta' scenario. Part of the thesis.

results.basis: The sub-basin count of the MARINA-Multi model configuration used — a property of the model domain, not an estimate.

results.claim: Identified the socioeconomic factors that dominate coastal pollution export
results.basis: Statistical analysis of model output against socioeconomic drivers. The finding is in the thesis; effect sizes are not restated here because they cannot be checked without it.

results.claim: Scenario storylines that turn model output into policy conversation
results.basis: Qualitative scenario method. Written to be argued with, not to be scored.

caseStudies.caveat: A pessimistic scenario is a device for surfacing what people would rather not plan for. It is not a forecast, and is not presented as one.

caseStudies.title: Flood-Resilient Wuppertal
caseStudies.subtitle: Keeping a city — and its suspended railway — out of the water next time
caseStudies.organization: Wageningen University & Research — Academic Consultancy Training
caseStudies.problem: Wuppertal's iconic suspended railway glides above a river that flooded catastrophically in 2021. The municipality asked: how do we keep the city — and the Schwebebahn — out of the water next time?
method: Led a six-person interdisciplinary team across climate science, engineering and policy.
Assessed flood risk to the city and its transport infrastructure using historical records, climate projections and GIS.
Facilitated stakeholder workshops to map the social drivers of vulnerability, not just the hydraulic ones.
Translated the analysis into an implementation roadmap the municipality could act on.

artifacts.name: Consultancy report — 'Becoming a Boat: Towards a Flood-Resilient Wuppertal'
artifacts.heldBy: Municipality of Wuppertal / Wageningen University & Research
artifacts.note: Delivered to the client under the Academic Consultancy Training programme.

artifacts.name: Flood cross-section — interactive
artifacts.note: The Wupper cross-section in the project dossier: slide the river from a calm day to July 2021 and watch the clearance under the Schwebebahn's hanging cars shrink.

results.claim: A complete flood-risk management framework delivered to the municipality
results.basis: The deliverable of the consultancy: accepted and presented to municipal stakeholders. Held by the client.

results.claim: Critical infrastructure vulnerabilities identified alongside cost-effective interventions
results.basis: GIS and climate-projection analysis, cross-checked in stakeholder workshops. Whether the recommendations were implemented is not something I can claim — that is the municipality's to report.

caseStudies.caveat: Advice delivered is not the same as advice taken. Nothing here claims an implemented outcome.

caseStudies.title: UN Disaster Risk Reduction — hazard data
caseStudies.subtitle: You cannot reduce disaster risk with messy data
caseStudies.organization: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR)
caseStudies.problem: UNDRR needed clean, comparable hazard information to support the Sendai Framework — especially for small island states, where one storm can erase years of development.
method: Audited Caribbean disaster-loss data against external datasets for the Sendai Framework Monitor and the Losses & Damages Tracking System.
Documented global hazard information systems, expanding regional and hazard-type coverage.
Standardised disaster-reporting terminology across sources, so economic loss and damage meant the same thing in each.
Built a risk-management factsheet for Trinidad and Tobago.

artifacts.name: Inventory of 54 global hazard information systems
artifacts.note: Contributed to the organisation's internal databases.

results.claim: 54 global hazard information systems identified and documented
results.basis: A count of the systems catalogued during the internship, recorded in the deliverable. Countable, not estimated.

results.claim: Regional and hazard-type coverage expanded by 25%
results.basis: Measured against the size of the organisation's existing catalogue at the start of the internship. The baseline is internal to UNDRR, so an outside reader cannot check it — which is why it is stated with its basis rather than on its own.

caseStudies.caveat: Internship deliverables sit inside the organisation. The counts are real and were recorded; the baselines they are measured against are not public.

caseStudies.title: Soft Path Water Management
caseStudies.subtitle: What if the answer isn't more pipes?
caseStudies.problem: Freetown keeps building bigger pipes, and keeps running dry. The uncomfortable question: what if the answer isn't more hard infrastructure at all?
method: Analysed Freetown's water-management challenges end to end, from supply through governance.
Developed soft-path alternatives: managing demand, capturing and reusing water close to where it is used, and community stewardship of the assets.
Evaluated feasibility specifically for resource-constrained settings, rather than assuming a European maintenance budget.
Packaged the result as an implementation framework other cities can reuse.

artifacts.name: MSc thesis — 'Approach to soft path water management: thinking beyond cement, steel and pipes', Freetown as case study
artifacts.note: Defended at Hunan University, May 2021. Available on request; not deposited in a public repository.

results.claim: Successfully defended at Hunan University, May 2021
results.basis: Degree awarded — MSc Industrial Engineering, 2021. The one fully checkable claim in this case study.

results.claim: A community-centred alternative to pipe-and-pump thinking, scoped for fast-growing cities in the Global South
results.basis: The thesis's contribution, as examined. It is a proposed framework, not a deployed one — no city has implemented it, and no cost saving is claimed.

caseStudies.caveat: This is a proposal that passed examination, not an intervention that was built. The distinction matters and is kept.

caseStudies.title: Groundwater Potential Mapping
caseStudies.subtitle: De-risking the drill bit in hard rock
caseStudies.role: BSc dissertation, then applied in the field
caseStudies.problem: The Freetown Complex is geologically stubborn — hard igneous rock where finding water is a gamble. Communities were paying for dry boreholes. The science needed to de-risk the drill bit.
method: Applied electrical-resistivity surveying to detect groundwater in hard rock.
Combined geological and hydrogeological data into GIS groundwater-potential maps.
Validated the predictions through field drilling campaigns — the only test that counts.
Produced siting recommendations for future boreholes.

artifacts.name: BSc dissertation — 'Mapping groundwater potential in the Freetown Complex: a geophysical approach'
artifacts.note: First class honours, University of Sierra Leone. Available on request; not deposited in a public repository.

artifacts.name: Groundwater-potential maps for the Freetown Complex
artifacts.note: Produced during the dissertation and used in subsequent siting work.

artifacts.name: Site the borehole — interactive resistivity profile
artifacts.note: A playable version of the reading the method depends on: read the curve, place the rig, drill.

results.claim: 70% aquifer strike rate in subsequent drilling
results.basis: Successful strikes as a share of boreholes drilled on sites selected with the survey method, during the Team & Team International fieldwork. Compared against roughly 30% for blind siting in the same geology — which is the comparison that makes the number mean anything.

results.claim: Method carried into 164 water points delivered across Sierra Leone
results.basis: 100 hand-dug wells rehabilitated, 50 boreholes constructed, 14 solar-powered boreholes — itemised, and summing to 164. The mapping informed siting; it is not the sole cause of the outcome.

caseStudies.caveat: The strike-rate comparison comes from field records, not a controlled trial. Geology varies between sites, and a good surveyor is part of the result.
